newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Guinness, GrandMet knock LVMH plan.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Guinness, GrandMet knock LVMH plan.

text.p: Britain's Grand Metropolitan Plc and Guinness Plc knocked down rebel shareholder Bernard Arnault's LVMH demerger proposal on Friday, saying it would result in tax costs of 1.5 billion pounds ($2.5 billion).

French luxury goods and drinks company LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton hit back quickly in what promises to be the most protracted and bitter Anglo-French tussle in corporate history, saying it would pursue its strategy of explaining its plan to investors.

The London market, accustomed to the war of words between both sides, took the latest twist in its stride. GrandMet shares closed down 9-1/2 pence at 609-1/2, while Guinness was unchanged at 598-1/2. LVMH shares in Paris rebounded from early falls, gaining 17 francs, or 1.05 percent, to 1,629.

LVMH chairman Arnault, who has vigorously opposed the proposed 24 billion pound merger between Guinness and GrandMet since it was announced in May, is pressing for a demerger of GrandMet's Pillsbury and Burger King food interests and of the Guinness brewing business.

He also wants to create a separately quoted three-way merger, DrinksCo, to include LVMH drinks division Moet Hennessey, Guinness drinks arm United Distillers and GrandMet's IDV. Arnault's proposal lays claim to a 35 percent holding for LVMH shareholders in DrinksCo, although he has since shown flexibility in this demand.

The Breton entrepreneur claims that his plan would produce cost savings of 65 million pounds ($108.9 million) over and above the 175 million pounds already identified by the British companies two-way merger. But in a strongly worded rebuttal of Arnault's proposal, the two British companies dubbed the claims as "unrealistic".

In a joint statement George Bull, GrandMet chairman, and Guinness chairman Tony Greener said: "Under LVMH's proposals our shareholders would end up significantly worse off than under the GMG Brands proposal.
"An immediate demerger would destroy rather than create value and we cannot countenance LVMH taking value from our other shareholders in the manner proposed."
They said the LVMH proposal was "fundamentally inequitable" and that LVMH's 66 percent share in drinks company Moet Hennessy was "not important to the success of GMG brands."
Both chairmen kept up a stony, unruffled tone at a news conference called to outline their defence, despite constant pressure from Arnault's tactical manoeuvres in recent weeks.

However, Guinness chairman Tony Greener told reporters that he was hopeful of reaching a solution with Arnault. "I very much hope there is a solution here. I think we have clearly talked about the criteria and we have already seen a degree of shifting on his part. You will notice he is no longer talking about 35 percent," said Greener.
"It is entirely in character that he would start with a very high demand," said Greener.

John McGrath, chief executive of GrandMet, told reporters that if LVMH took 35 percent of its mooted DrinksCo it would mean an "inequitable" shift in profits of 130 million pounds a year away from GMG Brands shareholders.
GrandMet chairman Bull described the problem as "a bit like the old tail wagging the dog."

He said that IDV, GrandMet's spirits arm, is already the world's largest spirits company and United Distillers, Guinness' drinks division, is number two, whereas if they involved Moet Hennessy brands, it would increase the spirits portfolio by three percent and the wine portfolio by six percent.
"They are tiny amounts in relationship to what we are talking about," Bull said.

McGrath told reporters de-merging Pillsbury and Burger King would mean a tax hit of 1.5 billion pounds. "Every investment bank has been at our door with proposals on how to get around that tax. Nobody has found a solution," he said.
U.S. law forces a non-domicile business group to pay a one-off tax if it sells or spins off a subsidiary.

But executives said they would still consider any future LVMH proposal that adds to the value created by GMG Brands and which provides for a fair sharing of that value amongst all shareholders.
Stock market analysts were impressed by the Guinness and Grand Met executives' spirited defence.

"I think there is a bit of positioning in the negotiating process at this stage but they have redressed the balance a bit in their favour after the PR (public relations) machinery of LVMH tipped it their way in the last few weeks," said Nick Lyall, an analyst at SocGen.

Analysts said their position was greatly strengthened by pointing to the onerous tax implications of Arnault's de-merger proposals and the fact the merger partners can change their plans so that only a simple majority of GrandMet shareholders is needed.

"I am certainly more confident they can get it through on their terms although it is always dangerous to under-estimate Arnault. So if they can they will still try and include him in the deal," said Nick Williamson, an analyst at Credit Lyonnais.
Under the current merger proposal, 75 percent of GrandMet shareholders need to vote in favour of it at an extraordinary meeting to be held in November.

But Guinness finance director Phil Yea told reporters this structure was chosen only to avoid 70 million pounds of stamp duty and could be changed to require only the approval of more than 50 percent of GrandMet shareholders.

Arnault has amassed a stake of about 11 percent in GrandMet in recent weeks, funded by selling Guinness shares, in the belief, analysts say, that GrandMet shares will give him greater influence in his effort to block the merger.

This has caused a divergence in Guinness and GrandMet share prices, with the former worth about 10p less at 600p than GrandMet shares. When Guinness and GrandMet announced the deal their share prices were equal.
LVMH is the largest single shareholder in both British firms with an 11.06 percent stake in GrandMet and 12.0 percent of Guinness.
But executives of both Guinness and GrandMet stressed that including LVMH's drinks arm Moet Hennessy would improve GMG Brands but it must be done at a price which creates value for all shareholders.

The LVMH demerger proposal for DrinksCo involves the acquisition of LVMH's 66 percent stake in Moet Hennessy for shares in DrinksCo and the folding of LVMH shareholdings in Guinness and GrandMet into further shares in DrinksCo.
Unlike GMG Brands' other shareholders, LVMH would therefore concentrate its holding into DrinksCo at the expense of other GMG Brands shareholders, executives told reporters.
A spokesman for Arnault's camp said the Guinness and GrandMet statement added "nothing of value to the situation", and was "simply a padded assembly of their releases to date."
Arnault, in London on Thursday, is expected to return here next week to visit more Guinness and GrandMet shareholders in an effort to win their support. ($ = 0.598 British Pounds)
